ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The intervertebral disc is a fibrocartilaginous cushion between vertebrae that absorbs shock, allows motion, and maintains spinal height. It is composed of a gelatinous nucleus pulposus and a fibrous annulus fibrosus.

sections.p: The intervertebral disc is a key spinal structure that balances flexibility and stability. It acts as a shock absorber, permits rotation and flexion, and keeps vertebral bodies separated.

Each disc sits between adjacent vertebral bodies, covered by hyaline cartilage endplates. The nucleus pulposus is rich in proteoglycans; the annulus fibrosus consists of concentric lamellae of type I collagen.
b: Annulus fibrosus: tensile strength, prevents herniation

sections.p: The disc lies anterior to the spinal canal and posterior to the vertebral body. It is adjacent to the vertebral endplates, facet joints, and the epidural space.
The outer annulus receives nutrition from the vertebral endplates via diffusion; the inner disc is largely avascular, relying on slow nutrient transport.
No direct innervation; pain arises from surrounding structures (facet joints, endplates) when disc pathology occurs.
Discs absorb axial loads, allow flexion/extension, and provide a cushion that protects vertebral bodies and the spinal cord.
Degeneration, herniation, infection (e.g., Pott disease), and trauma can compromise disc integrity, leading to pain, radiculopathy, or neurological deficits.
b: Pott disease: TB infection of disc and vertebrae

sections.p: Remember that disc degeneration is common in older adults but can be accelerated by obesity, smoking, and repetitive flexion. In low‑resource settings, TB of the spine is a frequent cause of disc destruction.
b: Disc space narrowing on X‑ray suggests chronic degeneration

sections.p: Treat underlying cause (e.g., anti‑TB therapy for Pott disease), provide pain control, and maintain mobility. Surgical intervention is reserved for severe neurological compromise.
Differential includes facet joint arthropathy, spondylolisthesis, and spinal stenosis. Disc pathology often mimics these conditions but is distinguished by imaging and clinical presentation.
b: Facet joint pain: localized, worse with extension

sections.p: Normal disc height on X‑ray may mask early degeneration; low T2 signal can be seen in dehydration or early TB. Clinical correlation is essential.
b: Early TB may appear normal on X‑ray

whenToSeekHelp: Severe back pain with fever or weight loss (possible spinal TB), sudden neurological deficits (spinal cord compression), or progressive kyphosis

faq.a: Degeneration weakens the annulus, and repetitive flexion or heavy lifting can force the nucleus pulposus outward.
In severe cases, a spinal fusion or disc replacement may be performed, but these are usually last resorts.

faq.q: Is disc degeneration normal with age?
faq.a: Yes, but lifestyle factors like smoking and obesity can accelerate it.
